newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian PM soothes lawmakers' fears over Chechnya.
newsitem.headline: Russian PM soothes lawmakers' fears over Chechnya.

text.p: Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin assured worried lawmakers on Tuesday that Russia would not let rebel Chechnya go and said a peace deal signed by security chief Alexander Lebed had not tied Moscow's hands.

"Russia's territorial integrity, its borders -- including internal ones -- the provisions of Russia's constitution are not up for bargaining," Chernomyrdin told the Federation Council (upper house of parliament).

The chamber, which comprises influential regional bosses, has been concerned that the deal struck by Lebed with rebels on August 31 effectively rubberstamps Chechnya's independence claim and leaves the separatists in control of the southern region.

"The agreement is being carried out only by the Russian side which is withdrawing troops from Chechnya," Council member Valery Kokov said, reading out a report by an investigative group from the chamber.
"Rebels have only consolidated their positions," he said.
"Russia is being squeezed out of Chechnya and a usurpation of power is taking place," he added after Chernomyrdin's statement.

Lebed and the rebels have agreed to defer for five years a decision on Chechnya's future political status -- the issue at the heart of the nearly two-year conflict which has killed tens of thousands of people.

Lebed said the deferral was needed to calm down hotheads on both sides, restore the region's economy and make its leaders more inclined to stick with Russia. The rebels have rather seen the deal as a face-saving way for Moscow to let Chechnya go.

"We have to give a clear and honest answer about whether Chechnya can become independent. And this will form a basis for further policy," Kokov said, indicating that Moscow was not happy to wait for five years.

Criticism of the peace deal in the Federation Council was much more subdued than the vociferous attacks it drew in the State Duma lower chamber last week, where it was described as "national capitulation".

Winning the support of the upper chamber -- which groups influential leaders from 89 Russian regions -- has always been more important for the Kremlin than the views of the boisterous but largely impotent Duma, which is dominated by the opposition.
Chernomyrdin praised Lebed for ending fighting in Chechnya but made clear this had been done on the orders of President Boris Yeltsin, who is now preparing for heart surgery.

He also made clear Moscow bore no responsibilities under the peace document. "There have been no agreements on Chechnya, no one has signed any agreements. There has been a framework of political declarations," he said, indicating that much work remained to be done.
Chernomyrdin said Moscow saw its main aim in Chechnya now as establishing a basis for a peaceful settlement.
He said Russia would focus on helping to set up a regional administration, demilitarising the region, rebuilding its social structures and preparing for free and fair elections.

"The future status of the Chechen republic as an integral part of the Russian Federation should be decided on the basis of the interests of the peoples of Russia and Chechnya through talks," Chernomyrdin said.

The Russian constitution does not allow any of its parts to secede. A change in the basic law allowing secession would require agreement from two-thirds of the Russian regions and involves a very long procedure that makes it highly improbable.
Lebed, who is currently meeting NATO officials in Brussels, brushed aside critics of his peace deal, who include Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov.
"The dog barks and the caravan passes," he told reporters in the Belgian capital, quoting a saying popular in Russia.
